newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: European feeds set to drift in Chicago's wake.
newsitem.headline: European feeds set to drift in Chicago's wake.

text.p: Physical meals and feeds trade in Europe faces a relatively quiet week, with no major crop data from the United States to dictate the market trend and direction largely left in the hands of speculative players in Chicago.
Traders said the market was slow to re-start after a three-day holiday weekend, with prices offered slightly higher and attracting little in the way of early buying interest.
"There are no special issues affecting the market this week, it's very quiet," said analyst Arie van Dijk of market statisticians Stigevo.

The market for products such as soymeal, sunmeal and rapemeal is still trying to find a true level with the end of the old crop approaching and the start of the new crop. Wild fluctuations in Chicago last week added to the caution here.
"Sellers are keeping prices high, but potential buyers are bidding substantially beneath them," one trader said.
Van Dijk noted prices for citruspulp and cornglutenfeed were coming under pressure, as arrivals in northern Europe gathered pace.
"Corngluten particularly has been expensive but with the arrivals in the next month, suppliers have no chioce but to lower their prices," he said.
Traders also pointed to another factor to favour caution.
Huge speculative interest in the coffee market, which has already led to sharp rally in prices in New York, may attract further fund business, sucking money from Chicago futures.
The idea that soybeans may be peaking could accelerate that migration, they said.
"It's certainly a possibility, they are the same funds (in coffee and soybeans)," Van Dijk said.
He also predicted a cooling off in prices in the U.S., with old crop beans coming down to around $7.50 a bushel and new crop easing back to $6.50.
In Europe, the recent rain has continued to ease fears of substantial grain crop losses, which traders cited as another bearish market factor.
